cards.front: What is the root of the collection hierarchy?
cards.extra: Map is not a Collection: it is a separate hierarchy because it stores key/value pairs, not elements.

cards.back: Sorted-set operations relative to a value: floor, ceiling, higher, lower, headSet, tailSet
cards.extra: TreeSet implements it. This is the API for "nearest match" queries on a sorted set.
TreeMap implements it — the workhorse for sorted key/value data.

cards.back: A double-ended queue: add and remove at both ends
cards.extra: ArrayDeque is the usual implementation. Use it instead of the legacy Stack class for LIFO work.

cards.back: It extends Vector, so every method is synchronized, and it exposes index-based access that breaks the stack abstraction

cards.front: What is the difference between Iterable and Iterator?
cards.back: Iterable can produce an Iterator; it is what makes a type usable in a for-each loop
cards.extra: Implement Iterable and you get for-each for free — that is the only thing the compiler requires.

cards.back: A utility class of static methods for collections: sort, reverse, shuffle, unmodifiableList, emptyList, singletonList
cards.extra: Do not confuse it with the Collection interface. This one only holds static helpers.

cards.front: How do you sort a list with a custom order?
cards.extra: Natural order needs Comparable; any other order needs a Comparator.

cards.front: What contract must a key of a hash-based map satisfy?
cards.back: equals and hashCode must agree: equal keys must have equal hash codes
cards.extra: Get it wrong and get(key) returns null for a key you know you put in — the classic HashMap bug.

cards.back: A Map<String,String> that can load and store itself as a .properties text file
cards.extra: It is the historical configuration format; the API is old (it extends Hashtable) but it is still everywhere.

cards.back: That callers cannot modify the list through this view — the underlying list is still mutable
cards.extra: It is a read-only view, not a copy. If the original changes, the view changes.

cards.front: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator?
cards.back: Comparable is implemented by the type (natural order); Comparator is a separate object supplied at the call site
cards.extra: One type can have only one natural order but any number of Comparators.

cards.front: How do you make your own class usable in a for-each loop?
cards.extra: The compiler desugars for-each into iterator(), hasNext(), next() — nothing else is needed.

cards.front: What is a Class<T> object good for in generics?
cards.back: Using a class as a runtime type token, so a container can check and cast per key
cards.extra: The pattern behind typesafe heterogeneous containers: Map<Class<?>, Object> plus casts inside get.

cards.front: What do generic wildcards make possible?
cards.back: Writing a method that accepts List<Integer>, List<Double> and List<Number> with one signature
cards.extra: List<? extends Number> — needed because generics are invariant, unlike arrays.

cards.front: What is the difference between List and Collection as a parameter type?
cards.back: List promises order and index access; Collection promises only iterability and size
cards.extra: Take the least specific type you actually use — often Collection or Iterable.
